source: Irving, Szegedy, Alemi, Een, Chollet, Urban (2016) DeepMath - Deep Sequence Models for Premise Selection
finding: First deep-learning premise selection. A premise is a library fact given to an automated prover (ATP). Task: given a conjecture and a huge library, rank facts so the prover sees only a small useful set. Framed as pairwise relevance of (conjecture, premise).
numbers: Corpus: Mizar Mathematical Library, 57,917 theorems; 32,524 (56.2%) have an E-prover proof used for training. Test: 2,742 held-out theorems. Earlier 14-method portfolio proved 40%; best single method 27.3%.
limits: Training labels come from ATP proofs, not human proofs; prior work found ATP-proof labels better when plentiful. Mizar only.
agent_relevance: The subgoal-library problem has the same shape: pick a small relevant subset from a large store given a goal.

source: Irving, Szegedy, Alemi, Een, Chollet, Urban (2016) DeepMath - Deep Sequence Models for Premise Selection
finding: Neural ranker beats the hand-featured k-NN baseline at small cutoffs. The prover is run on the top-k premises, k=16..1024.
limits: Gain is large at tiny k and nearly vanishes at k=1024: def-CNN is only +1.3 points over k-NN there.
agent_relevance: Selection quality matters most when context budget is small. With a big context window the gap shrinks.

source: Irving, Szegedy, Alemi, Een, Chollet, Urban (2016) DeepMath - Deep Sequence Models for Premise Selection
finding: Different selectors solve different problems. The union is far higher than any one method.
numbers: Union of def-CNN and char-CNN proves 69.8%; def-CNN plus k-NN 74.25%; all methods 2,218 theorems (80.9%); neural models alone 2,151 (78.4%). Two models also proved 823 Mizar statements not proved automatically before.
limits: Unions need many prover runs, so they cost more compute.
agent_relevance: Use several retrieval views (symbolic features plus learned) and union them when budget allows.

source: Irving, Szegedy, Alemi, Een, Chollet, Urban (2016) DeepMath - Deep Sequence Models for Premise Selection
finding: Hard negative mining was crucial: add as negatives the non-premises the current model scores high.
numbers: About 25% of mined negatives, rest random. Text reports successful proofs rose from 61.3% to 66.4% for the best neural model with mining.
quote: Negative mining was crucial for good quality
limits: The PDF text does not make clear which table this figure matches.
agent_relevance: Retriever training needs near-miss distractors, not random ones. For a subgoal library, keep near-miss failures.

source: Irving, Szegedy, Alemi, Een, Chollet, Urban (2016) DeepMath - Deep Sequence Models for Premise Selection
finding: Pairwise scoring avoids selecting a subset directly. Conjecture embeddings can be cached, so only scoring happens at query time. Metric: average max relative rank (aMRR).
numbers: Held-out 3,124 statements, 400 for monitoring. Test min aMRR: def-CNN 0.0575, char-CNN 0.0585, word-CNN 0.06, def-CNN-LSTM 0.0605.
limits: Differences between architectures in aMRR are tiny.
agent_relevance: Cached embeddings of stored items make library retrieval cheap.

source: Alama, Heskes, Kuhlwein, Tsivtsivadze, Urban (2014) Premise selection for mathematics by corpus analysis and kernel methods
finding: Founding modern machine-learning premise selection on Mizar: mine minimal proof dependencies, then learn which facts a conjecture needs. Compares naive Bayes (SNoW) and a new kernel multi-output ranker (MOR) with Vampire/SInE.
numbers: MPTP2078 benchmark: 2078 problems; average premises per problem 1976.5 unpruned, 74 heuristically pruned, 31.5 pruned by precise dependencies.
limits: Chronological setting; Mizar only; short time limits (5-10 s).
agent_relevance: Origin of the task as 'predict premises from past proofs'. Same logic applies to reusing past subgoal solutions.

source: Alama, Heskes, Kuhlwein, Tsivtsivadze, Urban (2014) Premise selection for mathematics by corpus analysis and kernel methods
finding: Learned premise ranking clearly beats the symbolic state of the art, SInE, with the same prover.
numbers: Vampire/SInE auto 548 solved; SNoW-70 556 (+1.5%); another SNoW run 722 (+31.8%); MOR-70 795 (+45.1%). Combined runs +44% and +50% over 548. Abstract: 50% improvement over Vampire/SInE.
limits: 10 s limit. One benchmark.
agent_relevance: A learned selector beat a hand-written relevance filter by a wide margin; the heuristic is the baseline to beat.

source: Alama, Heskes, Kuhlwein, Tsivtsivadze, Urban (2014) Premise selection for mathematics by corpus analysis and kernel methods
finding: Precise (minimal) dependency data matters. Ideal pruning to true dependencies lets the ATP solve more than heuristic pruning. Top-ranked premises cover most used ones.
numbers: With ideal pruning Vampire solves 1105 problems, 8% above heuristic pruning. About 88% of used premises within top 50 for one setting; about 80% in another (text lines near 969-971).
limits: Ideal pruning is an upper bound; real selection is not perfect.
agent_relevance: Label quality (what was truly needed) bounds retrieval quality. Log what a solved subgoal actually used.

source: Kaliszyk, Urban (2014) Learning-assisted automated reasoning with Flyspeck
finding: Whole-library bootstrapping test: prove each Flyspeck theorem using only earlier theorems and proofs, with learned premise selection plus ATPs.
numbers: 39% of 14,185 theorems proved in 30 s on 14 CPUs, push-button. 50% if HOL Light proof dependencies are given as advice. Joint 39.5% needed 192-fold combination of methods.
limits: Chronological simulation, not live use. Heavy parallel portfolio.
agent_relevance: Shows value of reusing a growing library of past results in time order, like a growing subgoal library.

source: Kaliszyk, Urban (2014) Learning-assisted automated reasoning with Flyspeck
finding: Too many premises hurts provers. Performance drops quickly past a few hundred premises.
numbers: One prover: 12.4% with 256 premises vs 6.2% with 740. Vampire: 18.1% vs 12.9%. E parallel stays above 20% at 512 and falls to 15.6% at 2048.
limits: Prover-specific; depends on translation.
agent_relevance: More retrieved items is not always better. Tune k for each consumer.

source: Kaliszyk, Urban (2013) MizAR 40 for Mizar 40
finding: Learned premise selection plus many ATP strategies proves 40.6% of 58,000 Mizar theorems in 30 s on 14 CPUs, with no user advice.
numbers: Training over whole corpus takes 1-3 s for efficient methods; 150,000 formulas. Earlier whole-library result was 18% (Vampire 0.6, 20 s). New best single method 27.3%, which is 50% more than 18%. 70 methods together solve 968 of 1930 problems (50.155%) on one subset.
limits: Mizar is regular and curated; may not transfer.
agent_relevance: Cheap, fast learners (k-NN, naive Bayes) scale to the whole library; retrieval need not be heavy.

source: Kaliszyk, Urban (2013) MizAR 40 for Mizar 40
finding: Iterative self-training: retrain the selector on ATP proofs found in the previous round. Success rises each round.
limits: Gains flatten after round 4.
agent_relevance: Bootstrapping a library from the agent's own successes helps, with diminishing returns.

source: Kaliszyk, Chollet, Szegedy (2017) HolStep: a machine learning dataset for higher-order logic theorem proving
finding: Dataset for HOL Light proof steps: classify each step as useful or not for the proof it appears in, with or without the conjecture.
numbers: 2,013,046 training and 196,030 test examples from 11,400 proofs; half positive, half negative (chance 0.5).
limits: Labels reflect mostly human-found proofs, so a model may copy human bias.
agent_relevance: Benchmark design: balanced useful-vs-not framing.

source: Kaliszyk, Chollet, Szegedy (2017) HolStep: a machine learning dataset for higher-order logic theorem proving
finding: Models did not use the conjecture. Conditioning on it gave little or no gain.
numbers: Unconditioned logistic regression 71% accuracy; unconditioned 1D CNN 82-83%; Siamese conditioned models did not beat unconditioned ones.
limits: Authors say the architectures could not exploit the conjecture; may be a model limit, not a task limit.
agent_relevance: Warning: a retriever may score 'generally useful lemmas' and ignore the goal. Test that it uses the goal.

source: Piotrowski, Urban, Brown, Kaliszyk (2023) Machine-learned premise selection for Lean
finding: Lean 4 + mathlib premise suggester with random forest and k-NN on names, bigrams and trigrams of theorem statements.
numbers: Cover (Cover+ allows 10 extra slots): all-premises filter, RF names+bigrams 0.57 (0.67) vs k-NN 0.52 (0.66); source filter RF 0.29 (0.36) vs 0.25 (0.36); math filter RF 0.26 (0.33) vs k-NN 0.23 (0.34). Premises per example 3.12 (all), 2.35 (source), 2.09 (math).
limits: Higher scores on 'all' come from trivial basic lemmas. Proof-state data (91,292 examples, 1.57 premises each): RF Cover 0.09 / Cover+ 0.24, k-NN 0.08 / 0.21; no significant gain.
agent_relevance: What counts as a premise changes scores about 2x. Define the target carefully.

source: Jiang, Li, Tworkowski, Czechowski, Odrzygozdz, Milos, Wu, Jamnik (2022) Thor: Wielding Hammers to Integrate Language Models and Automated Theorem Provers
finding: A language-model prover calls a hammer (Sledgehammer, which includes premise selection) as one action for low-level steps.
numbers: PISA/test (3,000 theorems): LM alone 39.0%, Sledgehammer alone 25.7%, Thor 57.0%. 8.2% of problems solved only by the combination. MiniF2F: Thor 29.9% vs prior 29.6%.
limits: Variants: 55.4% (-1.6) and 53.6% (-3.4) on PISA. Needs about 50 TPU hours per 1000 problems.
agent_relevance: Division of labour works: model for strategy, retrieval tool for fact choice. Calling a retriever as an operator beat both parts alone.

source: Mikula, Antoniak, Tworkowski, Jiang, Zhou, Wu, Piotrowski, Milos (2024) Magnushammer: A transformer-based approach to premise selection
finding: Contrastive transformer retriever (SELECT) plus reranker (RERANK) beats Sledgehammer and BM25 on PISA and miniF2F, single-step.
numbers: PISA: Magnushammer 59.5% vs Sledgehammer 38.3%; miniF2F 34.0% vs 20.9%. Compute budget 1000. Main model 86M parameters. BM25 and text-embedding-ada-002 were lower; ada-002 comparable to Sledgehammer.
limits: General OpenAI embeddings are well below Magnushammer, so domain fine-tuning matters. Sledgehammer budget is only approximate.
agent_relevance: Generic embeddings give a decent baseline; fine-tuned retrievers add a lot.

source: Mikula, Antoniak, Tworkowski, Jiang, Zhou, Wu, Piotrowski, Milos (2024) Magnushammer: A transformer-based approach to premise selection
finding: Combined with Thor it sets a new state of the art on PISA multi-step. The retriever lifts the whole agent.
numbers: PISA multi-step: Thor+Sledgehammer 57.0% to Thor+Magnushammer 71.0%. miniF2F valid/test: Thor+Sledgehammer 28.3/29.9, Thor+Magnushammer 36.9/37.3, Thor+SH+auto 37.3/35.2.
limits: Magnushammer budget 200 in these runs. The claim that it would help DSP too is only a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: A better retriever lifted the agent by 14 points on PISA without a bigger model.

source: Mikula, Antoniak, Tworkowski, Jiang, Zhou, Wu, Piotrowski, Milos (2024) Magnushammer: A transformer-based approach to premise selection
finding: Data and size: pre-trained model needs very little data; even a one-layer model beats Sledgehammer.
numbers: 0.1% of the MAPL data let the pre-trained model beat Sledgehammer and BM25. MAPL vs HPL data (38M model, budget 800): 56.3% vs 54.0%. Pre-training effect shrinks as data grows.
limits: Authors say dataset-source differences are subtle.
agent_relevance: Retrieval can bootstrap from a few examples with a pre-trained base; a small subgoal library may suffice.

source: Yang, Swope, Gu, Chalamala, Song, Yu, Godil, Prenger, Anandkumar (2023) LeanDojo: Theorem proving with retrieval-augmented language models
finding: ReProver: dense retriever limited to accessible premises plus a ByT5 tactic generator. Benchmark of 98,734 theorems from Lean mathlib with premise annotations, with random and novel_premises splits (test proof uses a premise unused in training).
numbers: Recall: BM25 R@1 6.7, R@10 17.2, MRR 0.15 (random); ReProver 13.5, 38.4, 0.31. novel_premises: BM25 5.9/15.5/0.14; ReProver 9.1/27.6/0.24. BM25 over all premises: 1.9/11.9/0.08.
limits: R@10 falls from 38.4 to 27.6 on novel_premises. Retrievers partly memorise premise use.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: retrieval works much worse for items not seen used before. Test on new items.

source: Yang, Swope, Gu, Chalamala, Song, Yu, Godil, Prenger, Anandkumar (2023) LeanDojo: Theorem proving with retrieval-augmented language models
finding: Retrieval helps proving, modestly. GPT-4 zero-shot is much worse.
numbers: Pass@1 random: ReProver 51.2%, without retrieval 47.6%, GPT-4 29.0%, tidy 23.8%. novel_premises: 26.3%, 23.2%, 7.4%, 5.3%. MiniF2F 26.5%, ProofNet 13.8%.
limits: GPT-4 may have seen the proofs, still lost. Retrieval gain is only +3.6 and +3.1 points.
agent_relevance: Retrieval is a real but small win for a trained prover. Do not expect big jumps from retrieval alone.

source: Yang, Swope, Gu, Chalamala, Song, Yu, Godil, Prenger, Anandkumar (2023) LeanDojo: Theorem proving with retrieval-augmented language models
finding: Two design tricks: retrieve only from premises accessible in the file, and use in-file premises as hard negatives. LeanDojo tooling also fixes a tool error: lean-gym judged 21.1% of correct proofs wrong, LeanDojo 1.4%.
numbers: Training ReProver took about 120 GPU hours (five days on one GPU).
limits: Gain from the tricks shown by ablation in the paper's Table 1.
agent_relevance: Restrict the pool to what is legal in the current context.

source: Zhu, Clune, Avigad, Jiang, Welleck (2026) Premise selection for a Lean hammer (LeanPremise / LeanHammer)
finding: LeanPremise, a neural selector trained for use inside a full hammer (Aesop + Lean-auto + Duper). Beats MePo, ReProver and random forest on Mathlib-test.
numbers: Recall@16/@32: LeanPremise large (82M) 63.5/72.7; small 59.2/67.8; MePo 22.1/22.3; ReProver 35.1/38.7. Proof rate (full / cumulative): no premises 16.9/16.9; MePo 19.1/19.1; ReProver 12.0/22.3; LeanPremise large 30.1/33.3; accumulated over sizes 37.3; union with MePo 37.6; ground-truth premises 43.0.
limits: Even perfect premises solve only 43.0%. Cumulative is an upper-bound style metric over settings.
agent_relevance: Retrieval has a ceiling. Combining neural and symbolic selectors raised the proof rate (union gain).

source: Zhu, Clune, Avigad, Jiang, Welleck (2026) Premise selection for a Lean hammer (LeanPremise / LeanHammer)
finding: Generalises beyond the training library and adapts to user-local lemmas. Compared with ReProver trained on the same splits.
numbers: Abstract: 21% more goals than existing selectors. 150% more theorems than ReProver (218M) in full setting, 50% more in cumul. Out-of-Mathlib (miniCTX-v2): share of ground-truth-solvable problems solved 79.4% vs 73.5% on Mathlib.
limits: Pipeline needs Lean-auto translation; some problems out of reach of Aesop and Duper.
agent_relevance: Selecting from the live context, including local definitions, matters for a growing library.

source: Petrovcic (2025) Combining textual and structural information for premise selection in Lean
finding: Adds a graph neural network over the dependency graph to the ReProver text retriever.
numbers: LeanDojo test: GNN-augmented R@1 17.98% (+33.98% relative), R@10 50.04% (+26.36%), MRR 0.4095 (+24.73%); with EMA R@1 18.31%, R@10 50.33%. Ablation: no ablation 17.43/48.52/0.4010; premise graph removed 17.45/49.30/0.4008.
limits: Baseline numbers differ from the original ReProver paper (different data version). Context-graph ablation matters little.
agent_relevance: Structure (which facts used which) gives a signal beyond text similarity. Link subgoal-library entries by dependency.

source: Gao et al. (2026) LeanSearch v2: Global premise retrieval for Lean 4 theorem proving
finding: Whole-theorem (global) retrieval: a sketch, retrieve, reflect loop recovers the premise set a whole theorem needs. Standard mode uses an informalised corpus plus embedding and reranker.
numbers: nDCG@10 0.62 vs 0.53 next best. 69-query benchmark: reasoning mode recovers 46.1% of premise groups in top 10, vs 38.0% for strong reasoning retrievers and 9.3% for stepwise premise-selection baselines. Downstream fixed prover loop: success 20% vs 16% next best vs 4% with no retrieval.
limits: Small benchmark (69 queries); downstream percentages rest on few items (about 25 or 50 problems implied by the round numbers).
agent_relevance: An LLM that sketches first, then retrieves, then reflects on gaps beats one-shot query retrieval. Fits retrieval inside the thinking loop.

source: Meng, Paulson (2009) MePo; Kuhlwein et al. (2012) MaSh
finding: Known baselines cited by the opened papers. MePo is a symbolic relevance filter based on shared symbols with the goal; MaSh is a learning-based selector in Isabelle. Not opened this session; only their use as baselines was read.
numbers: From opened papers: MePo Recall@32 22.3% on Mathlib (LeanPremise); Sledgehammer 38.3% on PISA vs 59.5% (Magnushammer).
limits: Original method details not verified from source text.
agent_relevance: Symbolic filters stay useful: unions with neural selectors raised proof rate (LeanPremise).
